(a) Annual Report on Intelligence.—Section 109 of the National Security Act of 1947 (50 U.S.C. 404d) is repealed. 
    (b) Annual and Special Reports on Intelligence Sharing With the United Nations.—Section 112 of the National Security Act of 1947 (50 U.S.C. 404g) is amended—
        (1) by striking subsection (b); and 
        (2) by redesignating subsections (c), (d), and (e) as subsections (b), (c), and (d), respectively.  
    (c) Annual Report on Progress in Auditable Financial Statements.—Section 114A of the National Security Act of 1947 (50 U.S.C. 404i–1) is repealed. 
    (d) Report on Financial Intelligence on Terrorist Assets.—Section 118 of the National Security Act of 1947 (50 U.S.C. 404m) is amended—
        (1) in the heading, by striking “semiannual” and inserting “annual”; 
        (2) in subsection (a)—
            (A) in the heading, by striking “Semiannual” and inserting “Annual”; 
            (B) in the matter preceding paragraph (1)—
                (i) by striking “semiannual basis” and inserting “annual basis”; and 
                (ii) by striking “preceding six-month period” and inserting “preceding one-year period”;  
            (C) by striking paragraph (2); and 
            (D) by redesignating paragraphs (3) and (4) as paragraphs (2) and (3), respectively; and  
        (3) in subsection (d)—
            (A) in paragraph (1), by inserting “the Committee on Armed Services,” after “the Committee on Appropriations,”; and 
            (B) in paragraph (2), by inserting “the Committee on Armed Services,” after “the Committee on Appropriations,”.   
    (e) Annual Certification on Counterintelligence Initiatives.—Section 1102(b) of the National Security Act of 1947 (50 U.S.C. 442a(b)) is amended—
        (1) by striking “(1)”; and 
        (2) by striking paragraph (2).  
    (f) Report and Certification Under Terrorist Identification Classification System.—Section 343 of the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2003 (50 U.S.C. 404n–2) is amended—
        (1) by striking subsection (d); and 
        (2) by redesignating subsections (e), (f), (g), and (h) as subsections (d), (e), (f), and (g), respectively.  
    (g) Annual Report on Counterdrug Intelligence Matters.—Section 826 of the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2003 (Public Law 107–306; 21 U.S.C. 873 note) is repealed. 
    (h) Biennial Report on Foreign Industrial Espionage.—Subsection (b) of section 809 of the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1995 (50 U.S.C. App. 2170b) is amended—
        (1) in the heading, by striking “Annual Update” and inserting “Biennial Report”; 
        (2) by striking paragraphs (1) and (2) and inserting the following new paragraph:“(1) Requirement to submit.—Not later than February 1, 2011, and once every two years thereafter, the President shall submit to the congressional intelligence committees and congressional leadership a report updating the information referred to in subsection (a)(1)D).”; and 
        (3) by redesignating paragraph (3) as paragraph (2).  
    (i) Table of Contents Amendments.—
        (1) National security act of 1947.—The table of contents in the first section of the National Security Act of 1947, as amended by section 332 of this Act, is further amended—
            (A) by striking the item relating to section 109; 
            (B) by striking the item relating to section 114A; and 
            (C) by striking the item relating to section 118 and inserting the following new item:


“Sec. 118. 
Annual report on financial intelligence on terrorist assets.”.

  
        (2) Intelligence authorization act for fiscal year 2003.—The table of contents in the first section of the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2003 (Public Law 107–306; 116 Stat. 2383) is amended by striking the item relating to section 826.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the many reporting and certification provisions amount to consultation, but every report here goes to congressional committees or leadership, which are inside the federal government. The section only repeals or modifies intelligence reporting requirements and updates tables of contents. No outside party such as a state, tribe, expert, company, or the public is involved in any federal decision, and there is no rulemaking, hearing, advisory body, or right to sue.
fable.s: the President shall submit to the congressional intelligence committees and congressional leadership a report updating the information referred to in subsection (a)(1)D).

qwen_block.w: This section mandates the submission of various reports to congressional committees and leadership. According to the definition, Congress and its committees are inside the federal government. Therefore, reporting to them is intra-governmental communication and does not constitute participation by outside parties. There is no requirement to consult with states, tribes, the public, or other non-federal entities before making a decision.
qwen_block.s: the President shall submit to the congressional intelligence committees and congressional leadership a report updating the information referred to in subsection (a)(1)D)
qwen_block.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the reports are about intelligence sharing with the United Nations or foreign industrial espionage, they involve outside entities. However, the definition explicitly states that reports to Congress are "inside the federal government" and do not constitute participation. The section only mandates the submission of reports to congressional committees or leadership; it does not require consultation with the UN, foreign governments, or the public before making a decision. The interaction is purely internal (Executive branch reporting to Legislative branch).

opus.w: The section only repeals or changes reports that federal officials owe to Congress and its committees, which are inside the federal government. Reporting to Congress looks procedural, but it never brings anyone outside the government into a federal decision. Nothing here requires consultation, hearings, comment periods, outside advisory bodies or a right to sue.
opus.s: the President shall submit to the congressional intelligence committees and congressional leadership a report updating the information referred to in subsection (a)(1)D).
opus.b: 1. **Analysis:** The tempting reading is that this is participation because it deals with formal reporting duties, including reports on intelligence sharing with the United Nations and a report to "congressional intelligence committees and congressional leadership." That reading fails the definition. Every report here goes from executive officials to Congress or its committees, and those are all inside the federal government. The section only repeals reports, changes how often they are due, and adds a committee to the list of recipients. No outside party (a state, tribe, company, expert or member of the public) is consulted, and no one outside the government gets a hearing, a comment period or a right to sue.

qwen_chat.w: This section mandates the submission of various reports to Congress, its committees, and congressional leadership. According to the definition, Congress and its members are inside the federal government. Therefore, these reporting requirements constitute intra-governmental communication, not participation by outside parties.
qwen_chat.s: the President shall submit to the congressional intelligence committees and congressional leadership a report updating the information referred to in subsection (a)(1)D)
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the reports are submitted to "congressional intelligence committees" and "congressional leadership," this involves interaction with outside entities. However, the definition explicitly states that Congress, its committees, and its members are INSIDE the federal government. Therefore, reporting to them is intra-governmental communication, not participation by outsiders.
